My great-uncle was 19 years old in 1945, a skinny kid named Jimmy who was raised on a ranch in Half Moon Bay, California. He joined the Marines and ended up in Easy Company, 2nd Battalion, 28th Marines, 5th Marine Division. On the morning of February 23'rd he found himself on a chunk of volcanic rock in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, a place were 6,800 of his fellow Marines would die over the short span of 36 days, Iwo Jima.

That morning, he and 40 other guys were given an order, to hike to the top of Mount Suribachi and plant a flag. No, this wasn't the flag immortalized by Joe Rosenthal in that iconic photo, this was the FIRST flag that went up that day. Unlike the guys in the famous pic, these lads were under fire from Jap snipers, and Uncle Jimmy's job was to provide cover fire with his M1 carbine while some of his buddies rigged a small American flag to a length of steel pipe that they found laying at the summit.

They accomplished the mission, but a few hours later some big-wig decided they needed a larger flag, one that could be seen from the entire island. Another bunch of guys went back up with Rosenthal and they posed for the picture that we all know. And I'm not knocking the second flag raisers, not by any stretch, they were still exposed to sporadic sniper fire, but it had pretty much subsided when they posed for that "official" photo.

Uncle Jimmy took a Jap bullet 9 days later, not fatal, but it was good for a ticket home. About the only time he talked about his war-time experiences was when he was drinking, which was fairly often. He told me that the fighting on Iwo Jima was barbaric, and that there was an unwritten "take no prisoners" policy...we always hear how the Japs refused to surrender, but the truth of that matter is that they didn't really have the option. The war in Europe was fought by the rules for the most part, the Pacific campaign was another thing entirely. American propaganda portrayed Japs as buck-toothed insects that needed to be eradicated, and the propaganda was VERY effective, especially with young Marines.

One story that sticks in my mind is the one he told me about the Jap who they found hiding in a cave one day. This guy had apparently had enough of the war, and he came out with his hands up, trying to surrender. My uncle's squad immediately open fired on the poor bastard, hitting him several times but not killing him. He retreated back into the cave, so they called up the dude with the flamethrower and incinerated him. Uncle Jimmy used to smile when he told that story.

So this morning I visited Uncle Jimmy's grave at the Massachusetts National Cemetery on Cape Cod and put some flowers on it. He had a good life, he always said that he liked to "drink, fight, and fuck", and he did plenty of it. He drank whiskey and smoked like a fucking chimney, and still lived to the age of 82. He always said it was gravy, every year that he lived after the war was a gift that 6,800 other kids who died on that rock never knew.

These guys really were the "Greatest Generation", honor them tomorrow.
